entities.name: Crystal Cathedral
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Crystal Cathedral in Garden Grove, California, completed 1980 and designed by Philip Johnson and John Burgee, is one of the most architecturally innovative religious buildings of the 20th century — a steel space-frame structure sheathed in 10,000 panes of silver-reflective glass, inspired by the star pattern of a diamond, that seats 2,736 people and was the home of Robert H. Schuller's 'Hour of Power' television ministry (the world's most watched religious television program in the 1980s-1990s, broadcast to 20 million viewers in 180 countries). The Crystal Cathedral represented the apex of American televangelism architecture.

Robert H. Schuller founded the Garden Grove Community Church in 1955, initially holding services in a drive-in theater (cars parked, services broadcast through speakers). The 'drive-in church' concept — which Schuller called his vision of a church accessible to California car culture — was his innovation before television. Philip Johnson's 1980 glass structure was the culmination of Schuller's 'possibility thinking' theology and his television ministry that made him the most televised American Protestant minister.

The Schuller organization went bankrupt in 2010 following internal family conflicts, excessive debt, and declining television ratings. The Crystal Cathedral and campus were sold to the Roman Catholic Diocese of Orange for $57.5 million in 2012 — converted into Christ Cathedral, the new Roman Catholic cathedral of the Diocese of Orange. The conversion of a Reformed Church in America congregation's landmark into a Catholic cathedral was a remarkable institutional reversal. Philip Johnson's glass structure was preserved with modifications; the campus has been restored to active worship.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Crystal Cathedral — the architectural apex of American televangelism, broadcasting to 20 million viewers in 180 countries from a 10,000-pane glass structure, then sold to the Catholic church after bankruptcy — encapsulates the rise and fall of 20th-century American Protestant media megachurch culture in a single building.
